orig_9709_m1_dyn_resultant.description: Use Newton’s second law on a single particle. Find acceleration, recover an unknown force and connect a force model to motion.

sections.title: Which force belongs in Newton’s second law?
sections.label: Find the signed resultant
sections.intro: Choose one body and decide a positive direction. Write the component of each force along that direction, keeping its sign. The sum gives a single resultant that describes the effect of all the arrows you have included.

blocks.html: Newton’s second law along the chosen axis is \(\sum F=ma\). The force on the left is the net force on the chosen mass. Use newtons for the forces, kilograms for the mass and metres per second squared for the acceleration.

figure.alt: A trolley has thrust to the right, resistance to the left, weight down and the normal reaction upwards.
figure.caption: The vertical forces balance while the trolley stays on the level surface. Use the two horizontal arrows to find the signed resultant.

blocks.html: If a driving force and a resistance both act, the driving force on its own is not the resultant.
Write the arrows or component signs before solving the equation. Check that the sign of the resulting acceleration matches the net force.

blocks.title: Use a different pair of forces
blocks.prompt: A \(6\, \mathrm{kg}\) instrument trolley travels right on a level test track. Take right as positive. Its driving force is \(29\, \mathrm N\) and its resistance is \(11\, \mathrm N\). Find the signed resultant and acceleration.
blocks.hint: Resolve in the direction of the track before applying the second law.
blocks.solution:
\(F_\mathrm{net}=29-11=18\) in newtons, because the thrust points right and the resistance points left.

\(a=3\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) by dividing the signed resultant by the trolley mass.

sections.title: Does a negative acceleration mean the trolley moves left?
sections.label: Separate velocity from acceleration
sections.intro: Velocity tells you which way the particle is travelling now. Acceleration tells you how that velocity is changing. They can have opposite signs while a particle slows. A positive velocity and a negative acceleration are consistent for as long as the velocity stays positive.

blocks.html: With right as positive, a larger resistance than thrust makes the acceleration negative. The fact that the trolley is travelling right fixes the direction of the resistance at that instant.
Do not turn a resistance arrow round simply because the acceleration is negative.
If you extend the motion beyond the instant when the velocity reaches zero, check whether your force model still applies.

blocks.title: Keep the sign of a slowing acceleration
blocks.prompt: A \(10\, \mathrm{kg}\) instrument trolley travels right on a level test track. Take right as positive. Its driving force is \(17\, \mathrm N\) and its resistance is \(32\, \mathrm N\). Find the signed resultant and acceleration.
blocks.hint: Resolve in the direction of the track before applying the second law.
blocks.solution:
\(F_\mathrm{net}=17-32=-15\) in newtons, because the thrust points right and the resistance points left.

\(a=-\frac{3}{2}\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) by dividing the signed resultant by the trolley mass.

sections.title: How can acceleration determine an unknown force?
sections.label: Write the force equation before solving
sections.intro: If the acceleration is known, mass times acceleration gives the signed resultant. This can help recover an individual force when the other forces are known. Label every unknown force as a magnitude with a direction, or as a signed component.

blocks.html: For thrust \(P\) and a leftward resistance of magnitude \(R\), use \(P-R=ma\). The minus sign is part of the component equation. A computed negative magnitude would contradict the assumed direction.
Substituting a negative acceleration into the equation does not mean changing the sign written for each force.
After solving, substitute every component back into the signed sum.

blocks.title: Recover resistance from positive acceleration
blocks.prompt: A \(11\, \mathrm{kg}\) instrument trolley travels right on a level test track. Take right as positive. The thrust is \(60\, \mathrm N\) and the constant acceleration is \(3\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the resistance.
blocks.hint: Resolve in the direction of the track before applying the second law.
blocks.solution:
\(60-R=11\left(3\right)\). The resistance contributes a negative component.

Solving gives \(R=27\, \mathrm N\). The answer is a magnitude and acts left.

sections.title: How do force and time combine in one question?
sections.label: Pass the acceleration into kinematics
sections.intro: Start with the force diagram, then find the acceleration. For constant forces and constant mass, acceleration in this model is constant. The motion equations can then use that acceleration and the given initial velocity or elapsed time.

blocks.html: For a fixed positive direction, \(v=u+at\) uses the signed acceleration and signed velocities. Check that the movement stays on the assumed branch if the resistance direction was chosen using the initial velocity.
The motion equations contain velocity and time, not the driving force.
Use the same axis in the force and motion equations so that the acceleration sign carries across.

blocks.title: Carry a signed acceleration into velocity
blocks.prompt: A \(14\, \mathrm{kg}\) instrument trolley travels right on a level test track. Take right as positive. It initially moves at \(5\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). For \(3\, \mathrm s\) the thrust is \(39\, \mathrm N\) and resistance is \(11\, \mathrm N\). Find its signed acceleration and the final velocity.
blocks.hint: Resolve in the direction of the track before applying the second law.
blocks.solution:
\(F_\mathrm{net}=39-11=28\) in newtons, because the thrust points right and the resistance points left.

\(a=2\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) by dividing the signed resultant by the trolley mass.

\(v=u+at=5+\left(2\right)(3)\) gives \(v=11\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

sections.title: What does steady velocity imply about forces?
sections.label: Check the zero-resultant case
sections.intro: A particle can move steadily while two or more forces act. Newton’s second law tells us that zero acceleration gives zero net force, which still allows nonzero individual arrows. At a stop or change in drive, write a new force sum for the new stage.

blocks.html: In straight-line motion, constant velocity gives \(a=0\). When the only horizontal forces are drive and resistance, this gives \(P=R\). Vertical balance should be checked separately.
Motion alone does not imply there is a nonzero resultant.
State the direction and any condition on the forces. A constant speed in the same direction in this linear model is constant velocity.

blocks.title: Calculate the force balance for steady travel
blocks.prompt: A \(11\, \mathrm{kg}\) instrument trolley travels right on a level test track. Take right as positive. Its driving force is \(31\, \mathrm N\) and its resistance is \(31\, \mathrm N\). Find the signed resultant and acceleration.
blocks.hint: Resolve in the direction of the track before applying the second law.
blocks.solution:
\(F_\mathrm{net}=31-31=0\) in newtons, because the thrust points right and the resistance points left.

\(a=0\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) by dividing the signed resultant by the trolley mass.

examples.title: Find a positive resultant
examples.question: A \(8\, \mathrm{kg}\) instrument trolley travels right on a level test track. Take right as positive. Its driving force is \(43\, \mathrm N\) and its resistance is \(11\, \mathrm N\). Find the signed resultant and acceleration.
solution: \(F_\mathrm{net}=43-11=32\) in newtons, because the thrust points right and the resistance points left.
\(a=4\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) by dividing the signed resultant by the trolley mass.

examples.title: Find negative acceleration during forward motion
examples.question: A \(12\, \mathrm{kg}\) instrument trolley travels right on a level test track. Take right as positive. Its driving force is \(18\, \mathrm N\) and its resistance is \(36\, \mathrm N\). Find the signed resultant and acceleration.
solution: \(F_\mathrm{net}=18-36=-18\) in newtons, because the thrust points right and the resistance points left.
\(a=-\frac{3}{2}\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) by dividing the signed resultant by the trolley mass.

examples.title: Recover an unknown resistance
examples.question: A \(10\, \mathrm{kg}\) instrument trolley travels right on a level test track. Take right as positive. The thrust is \(38\, \mathrm N\) and the constant acceleration is \(\frac{5}{2}\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the resistance.
solution: \(38-R=10\left(\frac{5}{2}\right)\). The resistance contributes a negative component.
Solving gives \(R=13\, \mathrm N\). The answer is a magnitude and acts left.

examples.title: Use force to predict a final velocity
examples.question: A \(9\, \mathrm{kg}\) instrument trolley travels right on a level test track. Take right as positive. It initially moves at \(4\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). For \(3\, \mathrm s\) the thrust is \(40\, \mathrm N\) and resistance is \(22\, \mathrm N\). Find its signed acceleration and the final velocity.
solution: \(F_\mathrm{net}=40-22=18\) in newtons, because the thrust points right and the resistance points left.
\(a=2\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) by dividing the signed resultant by the trolley mass.
\(v=u+at=4+\left(2\right)(3)\) gives \(v=10\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

examples.title: Recognise constant velocity with balanced forces
examples.question: A \(7\, \mathrm{kg}\) instrument trolley travels right on a level test track. Take right as positive. Its driving force is \(21\, \mathrm N\) and its resistance is \(21\, \mathrm N\). Find the signed resultant and acceleration.
solution: \(F_\mathrm{net}=21-21=0\) in newtons, because the thrust points right and the resistance points left.
\(a=0\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) by dividing the signed resultant by the trolley mass.

examples.title: Recover resistance while the trolley slows
examples.question: A \(11\, \mathrm{kg}\) instrument trolley travels right on a level test track. Take right as positive. The thrust is \(12\, \mathrm N\) and the constant acceleration is \(-2\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the resistance.
solution: \(12-R=11\left(-2\right)\). The resistance contributes a negative component.
Solving gives \(R=34\, \mathrm N\). The answer is a magnitude and acts left.

examples.title: Use exact fractional acceleration
examples.question: A \(12\, \mathrm{kg}\) instrument trolley travels right on a level test track. Take right as positive. It initially moves at \(6\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). For \(2\, \mathrm s\) the thrust is \(29\, \mathrm N\) and resistance is \(8\, \mathrm N\). Find its signed acceleration and the final velocity.
solution: \(F_\mathrm{net}=29-8=21\) in newtons, because the thrust points right and the resistance points left.
\(a=\frac{7}{4}\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) by dividing the signed resultant by the trolley mass.
\(v=u+at=6+\left(\frac{7}{4}\right)(2)\) gives \(v=\frac{19}{2}\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

glossary.definition: The signed total of the components of all forces acting on the chosen body.
The rate at which the signed velocity changes.
A force opposing the current motion in the model.
The direction used for positive component values.
A body modelled by concentrating its mass and forces at one point.

revision.body:

SituationCheck
Thrust and resistance\(P-R=ma\)

orig_9709_m1_dyn_vertical.description: Analyse vertical forces on a particle in a lift. Interpret readings, test the sign of acceleration and recognise loss of contact.

sections.title: Which forces act on a parcel in a lift?
sections.label: Select the body
sections.intro: Choose the parcel separately from the cage. The earth pulls the parcel downwards. The floor pushes it upwards as long as the parcel stays in contact. The cable force acts on the lift assembly.

blocks.html: With upwards positive, \(R-mg=ma\). The weight is \(mg\) and does not change just because the lift accelerates. The reaction changes to provide the net force required.

figure.alt: A parcel is supported by the lift floor. Its normal reaction R acts upward and its weight W acts downward.
figure.caption: Only forces on the parcel enter its force equation. The arrow marked upwards indicates the chosen positive direction.

blocks.html: Do not include the cable tension when resolving forces acting on the parcel alone.
Draw the parcel as a single point and label the positive axis.

blocks.title: Use the same rule with a different load
blocks.prompt: A \(9\, \mathrm{kg}\) parcel remains in contact with the floor of a lift. Take upwards as positive and use \(g=10\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). The signed acceleration is \(3\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the weight of the parcel and the normal force from the floor.
blocks.hint: Draw the forces on the parcel alone before resolving vertically.
blocks.solution:
\(W=90\, \mathrm N\) acts downwards and the reaction acts upwards.

\(R-mg=ma\). Keep the signs in this relation even if the lift is moving downwards.

\(a=3\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and \(R=117\, \mathrm N\) satisfy the vertical equation.

sections.title: How does the acceleration affect the scale reading?
sections.label: Interpret the sign of acceleration
sections.intro: Acceleration upwards requires an upward resultant, so the floor reaction exceeds the weight. Acceleration downwards requires a downward resultant, so the reaction is below the weight. The direction of motion is a separate fact.

blocks.html: If a lift is moving down and slowing, its acceleration is upwards. Use the stated acceleration or infer its sign from the change in velocity, then compare \(R\) with \(mg\).
A lift moving downwards does not necessarily have downward acceleration.
Write acceleration in words before using the sign in the equation.

blocks.title: Find the reaction for another downward acceleration
blocks.prompt: A \(18\, \mathrm{kg}\) parcel remains in contact with the floor of a lift. Take upwards as positive and use \(g=10\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). The signed acceleration is \(-2\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the weight of the parcel and the normal force from the floor.
blocks.hint: Draw the forces on the parcel alone before resolving vertically.
blocks.solution:
\(W=180\, \mathrm N\) acts downwards and the reaction acts upwards.

\(R-mg=ma\). Keep the signs in this relation even if the lift is moving downwards.

\(a=-2\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and \(R=144\, \mathrm N\) satisfy the vertical equation.

sections.title: What can a normal reaction tell us?
sections.label: Work backwards from apparent weight
sections.intro: A force scale under a parcel measures the contact force. Once its reading and mass are known, the acceleration can be found from the net vertical force. A scale calibrated in mass first needs to be converted using the gravity specified in the problem.

blocks.html: Rearrange \(R-mg=ma\) to get \(a=\frac Rm-g\). Compare the sign with the size of the reading and give the direction if asked.
A force reading is measured in newtons. It is not the mass of the object.
Substitute the answer back into the original force equation to check your sign.

blocks.title: Infer acceleration from a different force reading
blocks.prompt: A \(12\, \mathrm{kg}\) parcel remains in contact with the floor of a lift. Take upwards as positive and use \(g=10\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). The floor exerts an upward normal force of \(108\, \mathrm N\). Find the signed acceleration.
blocks.hint: Draw the forces on the parcel alone before resolving vertically.
blocks.solution:
\(W=120\, \mathrm N\) acts downwards and the reaction acts upwards.

\(R-mg=ma\). Keep the signs in this relation even if the lift is moving downwards.

\(a=-1\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and \(R=108\, \mathrm N\) satisfy the vertical equation.

sections.title: Can the floor ever pull the parcel down?
sections.label: Check the contact condition
sections.intro: A normal reaction from an ordinary floor is compressive. If the equation required a negative value, the assumed contact could not be kept. At the limiting state, the normal reaction is zero and the parcel accelerates under its weight alone.

blocks.html: At \(R=0\) the parcel has \(a=-g\) relative to an upward positive axis. If the lift floor accelerates down faster than free fall, the parcel loses contact and the two accelerations differ.
Do not report a negative normal reaction as though it were a downward force exerted by the floor.
Check the direction of the actual contact force even when the algebra is exact.

blocks.title: Reach the zero-reaction boundary
blocks.prompt: A \(13\, \mathrm{kg}\) parcel remains in contact with the floor of a lift. Take upwards as positive and use \(g=10\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). The signed acceleration is \(-10\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the weight of the parcel and the normal force from the floor.
blocks.hint: Draw the forces on the parcel alone before resolving vertically.

\(R-mg=ma\). Keep the signs in this relation even if the lift is moving downwards.

\(a=-10\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and \(R=0\, \mathrm N\) satisfy the vertical equation.

sections.title: When does the scale read the true weight?
sections.label: Separate steady and accelerating stages
sections.intro: During steady ascent or descent, zero acceleration gives equal upward and downward forces on the parcel. A change in speed changes the reading even if the direction of travel remains the same.

blocks.html: Write a new equation for each constant-acceleration stage. The weight is constant across stages. The reaction can be greater than, equal to or less than the weight.
A lift travelling steadily upwards does not require an upward resultant.
Describe the motion state and the acceleration state separately.

sections.title: Which axes make the force equations shorter?

blocks.html: For a slope at angle \(\theta\) to the horizontal, weight contributes \(mg\sin\theta\) down the plane and \(mg\cos\theta\) into it. Use the angle from the slope to determine which component is adjacent and which is opposite.

orig_9709_m1_dyn_connections.description: Solve linked-particle force equations using a whole system and an isolated vehicle. Distinguish rope tension from compression in a tow-bar.

sections.title: Why do linked vehicles have one acceleration?
sections.label: Start with the whole system
sections.intro: A taut inextensible rope or a rigid bar of fixed length keeps the distance between the vehicles constant along the line. During that stage the velocities, and therefore the accelerations, are equal on a common rightward axis.

blocks.html: For the combined system the connector pulls or pushes between its parts. Those forces cancel internally. Divide the sum of the external force components by the total mass to find the common acceleration.

figure.alt: Two vehicles are joined by a connector. It pulls the front vehicle to the left and the rear vehicle to the right. A drive arrow acts right on the front vehicle.
figure.caption: The connector forces act on different vehicles. For the combined system they cancel. Include all external resistances when finding the common acceleration.

blocks.html: Using the mass of only the lead vehicle with the external forces from both vehicles gives the wrong acceleration.
Show the assumptions supporting the common acceleration before combining the bodies.

blocks.title: Find acceleration of a new connected pair
blocks.prompt: Two vehicles move to the right on a horizontal line, joined by a light taut inextensible rope. The leading vehicle has mass \(9\, \mathrm{kg}\), thrust \(62\, \mathrm N\) and resistance \(17\, \mathrm N\). The rear vehicle has mass \(6\, \mathrm{kg}\) and resistance \(9\, \mathrm N\). Take right as positive. Find their common acceleration and the magnitude of the connection force. State whether the connection is in tension or compression, or exerts zero force.
blocks.hint: Combine the two vehicles to find acceleration, then isolate the rear one for the connector force.
blocks.solution:
\(a=\frac{62-17-9}{15}\) for the whole system. The connector forces are internal to this system.

On the rear vehicle, the signed horizontal force from the connector satisfies \(T-9=6\left(\frac{12}{5}\right)\).

The signed connector force on the rear vehicle is \(\frac{117}{5}\, \mathrm N\). Tension therefore has magnitude \(\frac{117}{5}\, \mathrm N\).

The force on the front vehicle from the connector has the same magnitude and the opposite direction in this ideal light model.

sections.title: Where does the connector force come back into the calculation?
sections.label: Isolate one vehicle
sections.intro: To find the connector force, use the force equation for one vehicle. It is now external to your chosen body. The rear vehicle often has fewer forces, which makes that equation simpler.

blocks.html: If the connector pulls the rear vehicle to the right, write \(T-R_2=m_2a\). Substitute the common signed acceleration. Use the front vehicle to check that the same magnitude acts the opposite way.
Using the whole pair to find tension makes the unknown disappear from the equation.
Label each resistance with the object it acts on. Carry the appropriate mass into the single-body equation.

blocks.title: Isolate the rear vehicle in a fresh model
blocks.prompt: Two vehicles move to the right on a horizontal line, joined by a light taut inextensible rope. The leading vehicle has mass \(15\, \mathrm{kg}\), thrust \(84\, \mathrm N\) and resistance \(14\, \mathrm N\). The rear vehicle has mass \(10\, \mathrm{kg}\) and resistance \(15\, \mathrm N\). Take right as positive. Find their common acceleration and the magnitude of the connection force. State whether the connection is in tension or compression, or exerts zero force.
blocks.hint: Combine the two vehicles to find acceleration, then isolate the rear one for the connector force.
blocks.solution:
\(a=\frac{84-14-15}{25}\) for the whole system. The connector forces are internal to this system.

On the rear vehicle, the signed horizontal force from the connector satisfies \(T-15=10\left(\frac{11}{5}\right)\).

The signed connector force on the rear vehicle is \(37\, \mathrm N\). Tension therefore has magnitude \(37\, \mathrm N\).

The force on the front vehicle from the connector has the same magnitude and the opposite direction in this ideal light model.

sections.title: How does a tow-bar differ from a rope?
sections.label: Interpret the sign of the connector force
sections.intro: A rigid bar can push as well as pull when the model keeps its length fixed. Let the force on the rear be positive forwards. A negative signed force means the bar pushes the rear vehicle backwards.

blocks.html: Positive connector force on the rear means tension in this orientation. Negative means compression, with magnitude given by the absolute value. A rope under a negative result would go slack instead.
Do not describe a negative magnitude as a negative tension.
Give both the magnitude and whether it is tension or compression.

blocks.title: Classify a fresh compressive bar
blocks.prompt: Two vehicles move to the right on a horizontal line, joined by a light rigid tow-bar. The leading vehicle has mass \(11\, \mathrm{kg}\), thrust \(0\, \mathrm N\) and resistance \(50\, \mathrm N\). The rear vehicle has mass \(9\, \mathrm{kg}\) and resistance \(10\, \mathrm N\). Take right as positive. Find their common acceleration and the magnitude of the connection force. State whether the connection is in tension or compression, or exerts zero force.
blocks.hint: Combine the two vehicles to find acceleration, then isolate the rear one for the connector force.
blocks.solution:
\(a=\frac{0-50-10}{20}\) for the whole system. The connector forces are internal to this system.

On the rear vehicle, the signed horizontal force from the connector satisfies \(T-10=9\left(-3\right)\).

The signed connector force on the rear vehicle is \(-17\, \mathrm N\). Compression therefore has magnitude \(17\, \mathrm N\).

The force on the front vehicle from the connector has the same magnitude and the opposite direction in this ideal light model.

sections.title: Can a connector exert no force during motion?
sections.label: Compare the independent accelerations
sections.intro: If the two vehicles would have the same acceleration when treated independently, no connector force is needed to maintain their separation. The connector can therefore exert zero force while both vehicles are moving.

blocks.html: Calculate the signed external force divided by mass for each vehicle. If these values already agree, the connected model gives zero connector force.
A decreasing speed does not automatically imply compression. The distribution of drive and resistance matters.
Compare the individual force-to-mass ratios to anticipate the sign before solving.

blocks.prompt: Two vehicles move to the right on a horizontal line, joined by a light rigid tow-bar. orig_9709_m1_dyn_pulleys.description: Solve smooth-pulley models with two hanging masses or a table and hanger. Use a new force equation when the string becomes slack.

sections.title: Why do the accelerations point in different directions?
sections.label: Choose a positive direction for each body
sections.intro: A smooth pulley redirects the taut string. As one side lengthens, the other shortens by the same amount. The two particles therefore have equal speeds and acceleration magnitudes, while their physical directions can be opposite.

blocks.html: For two hanging bodies, choose a positive axis downwards for the heavier one and upwards for the lighter one. This puts the same positive acceleration magnitude in both equations when the assumed motion occurs.

figure.alt: The lighter mass on the left has its tension upwards and weight downwards. The heavier mass on the right has the same upward tension and its own larger weight downwards.
figure.caption: Take upwards as positive for the lighter mass and downwards for the heavier mass. Both accelerations have the same magnitude.

blocks.html: Using one global vertical sign in both equations requires opposite signed accelerations. Do not combine a global axis with equal signed accelerations.
Mark a positive arrow next to each separate force diagram.

blocks.title: Change the masses while keeping the axis choices
blocks.prompt: Masses \(5\, \mathrm{kg}\) and \(9\, \mathrm{kg}\) hang on the two ends of a light inextensible string over a smooth fixed pulley. Use \(g=10\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and take downwards for the hanging \(9\) kg mass. Give the common acceleration magnitude and tension.
blocks.hint: The same string length fixes the magnitudes of the two accelerations. Choose a positive direction for each object.
blocks.solution:
Use a separate positive axis for each object. Take downwards for the second mass and upwards for the lighter mass.

The second equation is \(90-T=9a\). The first is \(T-50=5a\).

Adding cancels the tension. It gives \(40=14a\), hence \(a=\frac{20}{7}\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

Substitute that acceleration into one particle's equation. This gives \(T=\frac{450}{7}\, \mathrm N\).

sections.title: How can I find two unknowns from the force diagrams?
sections.label: Eliminate tension and substitute back
sections.intro: A light string over a smooth pulley has the same tension on both sides in this model. For the heavier mass, weight acts in its positive direction. For the lighter mass, the upward tension acts in its positive direction.

blocks.html: \(m_2g-T=m_2a\) and \(T-m_1g=m_1a\). Adding removes the internal pull. Substitute the resulting acceleration into either equation and check the other equation.
Using the weight difference with only one mass gives the wrong acceleration.
Find tension after finding the acceleration. The tension is a positive magnitude while the string stays taut.

blocks.title: Solve the same pair of equations at new masses
blocks.prompt: Masses \(8\, \mathrm{kg}\) and \(12\, \mathrm{kg}\) hang on the two ends of a light inextensible string over a smooth fixed pulley. Use \(g=10\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and take downwards for the hanging \(12\) kg mass. Give the common acceleration magnitude and tension.
blocks.hint: The same string length fixes the magnitudes of the two accelerations. Choose a positive direction for each object.
blocks.solution:
Use a separate positive axis for each object. Take downwards for the second mass and upwards for the lighter mass.

The second equation is \(120-T=12a\). The first is \(T-80=8a\).

Adding cancels the tension. It gives \(40=20a\), hence \(a=2\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

Substitute that acceleration into one particle's equation. This gives \(T=96\, \mathrm N\).

sections.title: How does a table change one of the equations?
sections.label: Keep the table resistance and hanger weight separate
sections.intro: For a box moving on a level table, only the horizontal forces enter its along-table equation. The box weight balances its normal reaction vertically. The hanging object's weight drives its downward motion.

blocks.html: Choose the box’s positive direction towards the pulley and the hanging mass’s positive direction downwards. Take resistance away from the pulley when the box moves towards it.
The weight of the block on a horizontal table does not appear directly as a horizontal resistance.
If friction is given through a coefficient, determine the normal reaction first.

blocks.title: Compute acceleration with a different table resistance
blocks.prompt: A \(12\, \mathrm{kg}\) box is on a horizontal table. A light inextensible string runs horizontally from it over a smooth pulley to a hanging \(8\, \mathrm{kg}\) mass. The resistance to sliding of the box is \(20\, \mathrm N\). The string is taut and the box moves towards the pulley. Use \(g=10\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and take downwards for the hanging \(8\) kg mass. Give the common acceleration magnitude and tension.
blocks.hint: The same string length fixes the magnitudes of the two accelerations. Choose a positive direction for each object.
blocks.solution:
Use a separate positive axis for each object. Take downwards for the second mass and towards the pulley for the box.

The second equation is \(80-T=8a\). The first is \(T-20=12a\).

Adding cancels the tension. It gives \(60=20a\), hence \(a=3\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

Substitute that acceleration into one particle's equation. This gives \(T=56\, \mathrm N\).

sections.title: How do I check that a result is physically possible?
sections.label: Check force directions and magnitudes
sections.intro: For two hanging particles with one descending, the lighter one rising requires tension greater than its weight. The heavier one descending requires tension smaller than its weight. These inequalities are a useful quick check.

blocks.html: When the table resistance exceeds the driving weight under the assumed configuration, the acceleration sign changes. Decide how friction is directed using the stated motion. If a particle starts at rest, the question may require a static-friction check first.
A negative computed acceleration does not justify turning all arrows around without examining the physical question.
Substitute into both force equations and check the sign of the tension.

blocks.title: Check the tension against both weights
blocks.prompt: Masses \(6\, \mathrm{kg}\) and \(10\, \mathrm{kg}\) hang on the two ends of a light inextensible string over a smooth fixed pulley. Use \(g=10\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and take downwards for the hanging \(10\) kg mass. Give the common acceleration magnitude and tension.
blocks.hint: The same string length fixes the magnitudes of the two accelerations. Choose a positive direction for each object.
blocks.solution:
Use a separate positive axis for each object. Take downwards for the second mass and upwards for the lighter mass.

The second equation is \(100-T=10a\). The first is \(T-60=6a\).

Adding cancels the tension. It gives \(40=16a\), hence \(a=\frac{5}{2}\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

Substitute that acceleration into one particle's equation. This gives \(T=75\, \mathrm N\).

sections.title: Which equations stop applying when the string slackens?
sections.label: Split the motion into constrained and free stages
sections.intro: A hanging mass hitting a support can end the common acceleration. If the string slackens, it exerts no tension. An object still moving can start its next stage with a nonzero initial velocity.

blocks.html: Find the boundary speed under the first acceleration. Use that speed as the initial speed of the continuing body. Redraw the forces and find its new acceleration. Use the constant-acceleration equations only within each stage.
Do not reuse the combined mass or tension in the second equation when the string is slack.
State the event that divides the stages and identify which body keeps moving.

blocks.title: Find the stopping distance after a shorter hanging drop
blocks.prompt: A \(10\, \mathrm{kg}\) block moves on a level rough table and is connected by a light taut inextensible string over a smooth pulley to a hanging \(5\, \mathrm{kg}\) mass. Set \(g=10\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). The block starts from rest, and the hanging mass is \(2\, \mathrm m\) above the floor. The constant resistance on the moving block is \(25\, \mathrm N\). After the mass reaches the floor the string becomes slack and the block continues without reaching the pulley. Give the first acceleration magnitude, the signed acceleration after slackening (towards the pulley positive), and the extra distance until the block stops.
blocks.hint: Find the speed at the floor impact, then remove tension from the block’s force diagram.
blocks.solution:
\((m_1+m_2)a=m_2g-R\) for the constrained stage, so \(a=\frac{5}{3}\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

As the hanging mass travels to the floor, the block advances the same distance. Use \(v^2=2a\left(2\right)=\frac{20}{3}\) in SI units.

Once the string goes slack, tension no longer acts on the block. Its new signed acceleration is \(a_2=-\frac{5}{2}\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

Apply \(0=v^2+2a_2s\) to the stopping stage. Its extra distance is \(s=\frac{4}{3}\, \mathrm m\).

As the hanging mass travels to the floor, the block advances the same distance. Use \(v^2=2a\left(2\right)=10\) in SI units.
